passage: The power cut hit the hostel just as Jasleen reached the corridor, and there on the stairs, lit by an emergency lamp, sat Rajni with her notes. Three days earlier Jasleen had told the whole floor about Rajni's failed audition, meant as a joke, and Rajni had not spoken since. Now the lift was dead and both had to climb to the fourth floor. Jasleen's chest tightened. On the second landing Jasleen said, "I'm sorry. I shouldn't have told anyone. There's no excuse." Rajni kept climbing, jaw tight. Jasleen wanted to add "please just say it's okay" and swallowed it. Instead: "I won't bring it up again. Take whatever time you need." At the fourth floor Rajni went into her room and shut the door softly, not slamming it. Jasleen stood in the dark, holding the weight of it.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen say sorry to Rajni?
qa.a: On the second landing of the stairs, while both climbed to the fourth floor during a power cut.

qa.q: What did Jasleen want to add after apologising, and why might Jasleen have held it back?
qa.a: Jasleen wanted to add "please just say it's okay" but swallowed it, probably sensing that asking for forgiveness would turn the apology into a request for Rajni to make Jasleen feel better.

qa.q: What would you advise Jasleen to do over the next few weeks?
qa.a: Give Rajni space, stay courteous, and not raise the subject again unless Rajni does, accepting that repair is Rajni's choice and may take time. 🤍

qa.q: How might Rajni have experienced the apology on the stairs?
qa.a: Rajni may have noticed that it named the wrong without excuses, yet still felt too hurt to answer. Closing the door softly instead of slamming it suggests the words were heard.

grounding: Shows the person harmed refusing to speak while the one who hurt apologises without excuses, gives space and leaves forgiveness to her.

At the housewarming in their Pune flat, Rehana had pulled out Devika's old poetry notebook and read a love poem aloud, doing a silly voice. Everyone laughed. Devika walked out of the room.

That was nine days ago. Since then Devika left for work early, came back late, and walked past Rehana in the kitchen as if she were furniture.

The weight of it sat on Rehana's chest every morning. On the tenth day she wrote a note and slid it under Devika's door: "I read your poem to get a laugh. It was cruel and it was your private writing. I'm sorry. There's no excuse. I won't push you to talk. When and if you want to, I'm here."

Devika didn't answer. Rehana badly wanted to knock, to plead. She didn't. She cleaned the kitchen, paid her share of the bills, and waited. On the fifteenth day there was a cup of tea outside her door.

qa.q: What did Rehana read aloud at the housewarming?
qa.a: Rehana read a love poem from Devika's old poetry notebook, doing a silly voice.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling during the days of silence?
qa.a: Rehana felt guilty and heavy, with the weight of what she had done sitting on her chest every morning.

qa.q: What was wise about Rehana's apology?
qa.a: It named exactly what she did, made no excuses, and left the choice to talk with Devika instead of pressing her.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt at the housewarming?
qa.a: Devika likely felt humiliated and betrayed, having her private writing mocked in front of everyone.

grounding: The story shows a young woman whose friend refuses to speak to her after being hurt, apologising clearly without excuses and giving space.

"Payal, can I talk to you for two minutes?"

"No, Wasim."

"Please. I just want to say sorry properly."

Payal put her bag down on the library table. "You imitated my stammer in front of the whole seminar group. Everyone laughed. You laughed loudest."

"I know. It was cruel. I'm sorry. I don't have an excuse."

"You said sorry on Tuesday too."

"I did. I'm not asking you to forgive me. I just wanted you to hear it without me trying to explain."

She looked at him for a long time. "I'm still angry. I don't want to talk to you for a while."

Wasim's chest felt heavy. He wanted to argue, to say he'd changed. "Okay," he said. "That's your choice."

He went to the other end of the library. In the next seminar, when someone else laughed at a classmate's accent, Wasim said quietly, "Don't."

qa.q: What did Wasim imitate in front of the seminar group?
What was Wasim feeling when Payal said she didn't want to talk?
qa.a: Wasim felt a heavy chest and the urge to argue, carrying the weight of the harm he had done.

qa.q: Why was Wasim right to accept Payal's choice?
qa.a: Repair is her choice and takes time, so pressing for forgiveness would hurt her again; he showed change through his actions instead.

qa.q: How does Payal see Wasim's second apology?
qa.a: Payal is still angry and wary, since he apologised before, and she needs time before she can talk to him.

grounding: The dialogue shows a young man whose apology is refused by the young woman he hurt, apologising without excuses, giving space and accepting her choice.
